item.title: Speed Over Rate: Why Experienced Portfolio Investors Think About Finance Differently
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

When it comes to property investment, seasoned portfolio landlords often prioritise different mortgage factors compared to those just starting out. While new investors may focus solely on securing the lowest interest rate, experienced investors with multiple properties frequently value speed and flexibility above all else.

The Speed Versus Rate Trade-Off

For landlords managing extensive property portfolios, the ability to move quickly on new opportunities can outweigh marginal differences in interest rates. A slightly higher-rate mortgage that completes within weeks rather than months might represent better value when properties are in high demand. This approach acknowledges that delayed financing could mean missing out on prime investments altogether.

Several factors contribute to this mindset among portfolio landlords:

  • Competition for high-yielding properties in sought-after locations
  • The need to complete before competing buyers
  • The financial impact of void periods when waiting for finance
  • Opportunity costs of delayed investment decisions

Specialist Lending Solutions

Many portfolio investors turn to specialist lenders who understand the need for swift transactions. While these products might carry slightly higher rates than standard buy-to-let mortgages, they often offer:

  • Faster application processing times
  • More flexible underwriting criteria
  • Higher loan-to-value ratios for portfolio cases
  • Bespoke lending solutions for complex scenarios

Some specialist lenders have dedicated teams for portfolio landlords, streamlining the approval process while maintaining robust credit checks. This balance between speed and responsible lending makes them particularly attractive to experienced investors.

For investors considering this approach, it could be worth discussing options with a whole-of-market mortgage broker who understands both mainstream and specialist lending markets. They can help weigh up whether a potentially higher-rate mortgage with faster completion might better serve long-term portfolio growth objectives.

item.title: Commonhold reforms face major practical hurdles, property experts warn
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Property experts have raised significant concerns over the practical implementation of the government's proposed commonhold reforms, highlighting potential hurdles around mortgage lending, management costs and conversion processes. The warnings emerged during discussions at the recent Association of Leasehold Enfranchisement Practitioners (ALEP) conference, where industry professionals examined the draft Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill.

Mortgage lending and conversion costs raise concerns

The government's plans to make commonhold the default tenure for new flats and simplify conversions for existing leaseholders face several financial challenges. Industry professionals noted that unclear funding mechanisms for conversions could create barriers, particularly when some leaseholders may struggle to contribute financially. The treatment of existing mortgages under the new system also requires clarification to maintain lender confidence.

Mark Chick, director at ALEP, emphasised that successful reform would require coordinated preparation across the property sector. This includes establishing robust systems for property registration, mortgage provision and ongoing financial management. Lenders will need assurance that commonhold properties offer sufficient security before offering mortgage products, while residents taking control of buildings must fully understand their financial responsibilities.

Management responsibilities under commonhold

Delegates at the conference highlighted that building maintenance obligations remain unchanged regardless of ownership structure. Commonhold associations will need to establish effective systems for collecting contributions, maintaining reserve funds and handling day-to-day management. The reforms must address how these associations will enforce payment collection and ensure buildings meet all safety and regulatory requirements.

The discussions also covered how the proposed commonhold system would interact with provisions from the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024. Contributions from representatives across the sector, including major lenders and property firms, examined practical considerations around valuations, collective enfranchisement and recent legal developments.

While the move towards commonhold aims to give homeowners greater control, industry experts stress that successful implementation will depend on addressing these practical challenges. The government will need to work closely with lenders, managing agents and legal professionals to create a system that works for all stakeholders while protecting homeowners' interests.

item.title: Rogue agents exposed in BBC investigation
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A recent BBC Panorama investigation has brought to light concerning practices within the UK’s supported exempt accommodation (SEA) sector, raising questions about the exploitation of vulnerable tenants and potential misuse of housing benefits. The programme, which aired on BBC One and is available on BBC iPlayer, highlighted allegations of inadequate tenant support, suspected benefit fraud, and instances where housing benefit claims were made for individuals who were not residing in the properties.

Supported exempt accommodation is designed to house vulnerable groups, including domestic abuse survivors, former prisoners, and those recovering from addiction. In Birmingham alone, the Department for Work and Pensions allocated £410 million to SEA in the last financial year, with over 34,000 individuals living in such properties across the city. However, the investigation suggests that some managing agents may be prioritising profits over the welfare of tenants.

Concerns Over Tenant Support

The Panorama team focused on Second City Support Ltd, a managing agent overseeing a Birmingham property on behalf of Dawson Housing. Dawson Housing received £443 per week in housing benefit for one tenant, Alysha, who had sought refuge from domestic abuse. Alysha claimed she received minimal support and endured an eight-day period without heating or hot water. While Dawson Housing disputed these allegations, citing regular face-to-face assistance, their lawyers acknowledged some communication issues but denied any prolonged heating outage.

In addition to concerns over tenant support, the investigation raised questions about the financial practices of some managing agents. Darren Davey, owner of Second City Housing Properties and other companies, came under scrutiny. Land Registry records revealed that one property managed by his company was purchased for £191,000 in 2024 and sold for £410,000 just a year later. Davey explained that significant renovation costs justified the sale price, but BBC analysis also showed he received £2.9 million in dividends and over £900,000 in salary across three financial years. Davey emphasised that these earnings were linked to his broader business interests, not solely supported accommodation.

Ghost Tenants and Benefit Fraud

Perhaps the most alarming discovery was the alleged practice of using “ghost tenants” to claim housing benefits. Panorama uncovered advertisements on social media platforms, including Facebook, seeking individuals whose details could be used to support benefit claims without them actually occupying the properties. Such practices, if proven, would constitute serious fraud and undermine the integrity of the housing benefit system.

The investigation also highlighted how some managing agents have used incentives like free rooms, games consoles, and even holidays to attract tenants. While these offers may appear appealing, they raise ethical concerns about the motivations behind them and the potential exploitation of vulnerable individuals.

As the findings of the Panorama investigation continue to spark debate, homeowners and tenants alike may wish to remain vigilant about the practices of managing agents and housing providers. For those navigating the SEA sector, understanding their rights and seeking independent advice could prove invaluable in ensuring fair treatment and support.

item.title: Chancellor rules out capital gains tax rise ahead of Budget
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Property investors and second-home owners can breathe a sigh of relief as Chancellor John Healey confirms Capital Gains Tax (CGT) rates will remain unchanged in next week’s Budget. The decision follows speculation that the Treasury might align CGT with income tax rates, which could have significantly increased tax liabilities for landlords and property sellers.

Stability for property investors

The Chancellor’s confirmation maintains the current CGT structure, where higher-rate taxpayers face a 24% rate on residential property gains, while basic-rate taxpayers typically pay 18%. These rates remain considerably lower than the 45% additional income tax rate applied in most of the UK.

Property professionals have welcomed the decision, noting that stable CGT rates provide clarity for:

  • Buy-to-let landlords considering portfolio adjustments
  • Owners of second homes contemplating sales
  • Property investors making long-term financial plans

Some experts suggest the move may encourage more property transactions in the coming months, as sellers no longer face the prospect of imminent tax increases on their capital gains.

Economic considerations behind the decision

Treasury analysis reportedly influenced the Chancellor’s decision, with officials warning that higher CGT rates could backfire economically. Research indicates that increasing the higher CGT rate by 10 percentage points might actually reduce government revenues by approximately £3.6 billion by 2028-29.

Key concerns included:

  • The potential for investors to delay property sales indefinitely
  • The risk of wealthy individuals relocating overseas
  • Negative impacts on business investment confidence

Former Goldman Sachs chief economist Lord Jim O’Neill publicly opposed CGT increases, arguing they would send damaging signals to the business community during a period of economic uncertainty.

Looking ahead to Budget announcements

While the CGT decision provides certainty in one area, property owners should remain alert for other potential tax changes when the Chancellor delivers his Budget on 28 October. The Treasury may still introduce adjustments to property taxation through alternative measures.

Financial advisers recommend that landlords and investors review their portfolios in light of the confirmed CGT position, as those considering property sales might find the current tax regime more favourable than potential future changes. As always, seeking professional tax advice tailored to individual circumstances remains crucial when making significant financial decisions.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent developments in the UK property sector highlight significant leadership changes and strategic moves aimed at enhancing market expertise and lead generation. Two prominent estate agencies, Chestertons and Moveli, have announced key appointments that could reshape their operations in Central London and beyond.

Chestertons Promotes Andrew Chrysanthou to Regional Director

Chestertons has appointed Andrew Chrysanthou as the new regional director of Central London lettings. With over 15 years of experience in the property industry, Chrysanthou brings a wealth of knowledge to the role. He joined Chestertons nine years ago and has since played a pivotal part in the success of the agency’s Knightsbridge lettings business.

In his new position, Chrysanthou will oversee lettings teams across Central London, focusing on strengthening landlord relationships and driving business development. His career began as a negotiator in 2009, and prior to joining Chestertons, he held branch management roles at Cluttons and Barnard Marcus, covering areas such as Clapham, Fulham, and Earl’s Court.

Commenting on his promotion, Chrysanthou said, “Central London is a diverse market, and landlords and tenants value clear advice from professionals who understand their neighbourhoods. With tenant demand on the rise, I’m excited to work with our teams to build on their local expertise.”

Katinka Hill, head of lettings at Chestertons, praised Chrysanthou’s contributions, stating, “Andrew has been instrumental in the success of our Knightsbridge operations. His deep market knowledge and leadership skills make him the ideal candidate for this role.”

Moveli Appoints Tristan Redburn to Lead New Business Department

Meanwhile, Moveli has announced the appointment of Tristan Redburn to head its newly established business development department. Redburn joins Moveli after eight years at Hamptons, where he led a team that generated £12 million in revenue for the wider network.

Moveli, which recently surpassed 100 brokers, has launched this department to enhance lead generation and prospecting activities. The agency currently distributes over 100 seller leads monthly, and the new team aims to increase this figure through targeted prospecting and leveraging brokers’ existing client databases.

Redburn’s role will involve reconnecting with former clients, applicants, and valuation prospects to identify potential sellers. Brokers will retain control over their client relationships while benefiting from Moveli’s expanded lead generation capabilities. The agency also plans to integrate advanced technologies, including automation and AI, into its Moveli OS platform to streamline these processes.

Ben Littlewood, co-founder of Moveli, expressed confidence in Redburn’s appointment, highlighting his proven track record in business development and his ability to drive growth.

These strategic appointments reflect the evolving nature of the UK property market, with agencies investing in leadership and technology to meet growing demand and enhance client services. Homeowners and landlords may find these developments indicative of a more competitive and dynamic market landscape.

item.title: Estate agents demand housing market boost as Budget scepticism grows
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

As the Autumn Budget approaches, concerns are mounting among estate agents about the government’s ability to provide meaningful support for the UK housing market. Despite recent initiatives aimed at first-time buyers, a survey by GetAgent reveals that 84% of agents lack confidence in housing featuring prominently in the Budget. This scepticism comes amidst a challenging year for the property sector, with over half of agents (56%) reporting that the market has performed worse than expected in 2026.

Market Performance and Government Intervention

The survey highlights widespread dissatisfaction with current market conditions. While 37% of agents noted that activity has broadly matched expectations, only 7% reported a stronger performance. Furthermore, 58% of respondents believe that existing government measures have failed to improve the market, with just 12% considering them effective. This sentiment underscores calls for more substantial intervention, as 68% of agents argue that a government-led boost is needed to stimulate activity.

First-time buyers remain a key focus for agents, with 40% identifying this group as the most urgently in need of support. Landlords and property investors followed at 29%, while existing homeowners looking to move accounted for 14%. Tenants were prioritised by just 10% of respondents. In response to these concerns, the government recently announced the Your First Home scheme, which aims to assist first-time buyers in England by offering a deposit as low as 2.5% alongside a 20% government-backed equity loan.

Call for Broader Market Support

While the Your First Home scheme addresses one of the industry’s main concerns, questions remain about whether the Budget will include wider measures to support housing transactions. Colby Short, co-founder and CEO of GetAgent, acknowledged the announcement as a step in the right direction but emphasised the need for broader action. “The government has identified an area where agents believe intervention is most urgently needed,” he said. “However, agents clearly believe more needs to be done to stimulate the wider market.”

The property industry is calling for comprehensive measures that go beyond first-time buyer incentives. With market activity remaining subdued, agents are urging the government to implement strategies that will boost confidence and encourage transactions across all buyer groups. As the Budget announcement looms, the sector awaits clarity on whether policymakers will heed these calls.

With the housing market at a crossroads, the Autumn Budget presents a crucial opportunity for the government to address these concerns and introduce measures that could reinvigorate the property sector. Homeowners, buyers, and industry professionals alike will be watching closely to see if the Budget delivers the support needed to drive market activity forward.

item.title: Prime London rental yields hit 17-year high as landlords weigh their options
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Rental yields in prime central London have reached their highest level in over 15 years, according to recent data. Rising rents combined with softer property values are creating favourable conditions for landlords, particularly in the capital’s most sought-after locations. However, regulatory changes and tax pressures continue to weigh heavily on the sector, potentially impacting the availability of rental properties.

Prime London Rental Growth Accelerates

Figures from Savills indicate that prime central London rents increased by 1.1% in the third quarter of 2026, marking the strongest quarterly growth in two years. Over the past year, rents in this area have risen by 1.9%. Meanwhile, outer prime London saw a 0.9% quarterly increase, bringing annual rental inflation to 2.9%. This growth is partly driven by a reduction in rental supply, particularly for properties with annual rents below £100,000, which has intensified competition among tenants.

The Renters’ Rights Act, introduced in recent years, has been identified as a key concern for landlords. Nearly half of Savills’ agents highlighted the legislation as a significant issue, alongside increased taxation on property income and rising mortgage costs. These factors have led to heightened caution among landlords, with some reassessing their portfolios and, in some cases, exiting the market altogether.

Smaller Properties Deliver Stronger Yields

Smaller properties, particularly one-bedroom flats, are currently offering the highest rental yields in prime London. Gross yields for these apartments average 5.8%, while yields across prime London flats generally exceed 4%. This trend is attributed to rising rents and a decline in capital values, which have pushed average yields in prime central London to their highest level since 2009.

Despite these strong yields, landlords should be mindful of additional costs, such as higher mortgage rates, maintenance expenses, and compliance with regulatory requirements. These factors can erode net returns, even in a high-yield environment. For those considering retaining their rental properties, it could be worth seeking professional advice to navigate the complex landscape effectively.

Regional Rental Growth Remains Subdued

Outside London, prime rental growth has been far more modest. In the third quarter of 2026, average rents across prime regional markets increased by just 0.3%. This slower pace reflects broader economic pressures and a more balanced supply-demand dynamic in these areas. For landlords operating outside the capital, the focus may need to shift towards maximising occupancy and maintaining property appeal to attract tenants.

As the rental market continues to evolve, landlords might consider reviewing their strategies to adapt to changing conditions. Whether in prime London or regional markets, staying informed about regulatory developments and market trends could help ensure long-term success in the sector.

While higher yields in prime central London present opportunities, landlords must weigh these against the challenges of increased taxation and regulatory scrutiny. With careful planning and a proactive approach, property investors may find ways to navigate this complex landscape effectively.

item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:

item.title: Only 25% of £2m homes sell and take twice as long
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New research highlights significant challenges in the premium property market, with only one in four £2 million homes successfully selling and transactions taking twice as long to complete compared to lower-value properties. Meanwhile, demand for flats continues to weaken across the UK housing market.

Luxury home sales face extended delays

Analysis by TwentyCi reveals that high-end properties priced at £2 million or above experience notably slower sales, with just 25% of listed homes achieving a sale. These premium properties typically spend around six months on the market before finding a buyer – double the average time for more affordable homes.

The research also indicates that sellers in this price bracket often need to reduce their asking prices to secure interest, with larger discounts becoming increasingly common. Whilst the exact discount figures vary by location, some prime postcodes have seen reductions exceeding 10% from the initial listing price.

Flat demand continues downward trend

Separately, the data shows the ongoing decline in demand for flats, a trend that has persisted for several quarters. Multiple factors may be contributing to this shift, including:

  • Changing priorities among buyers post-pandemic, with more space becoming a priority
  • Concerns over cladding issues and associated costs
  • Higher service charges in many apartment buildings
  • Restricted availability of mortgages for certain flat types

This sustained downturn in the flat market could prompt some sellers to reconsider their pricing strategies or explore alternative options such as renting out their properties instead.

Regional variations in the premium market

The challenges facing £2 million+ properties aren't uniform across the country. Certain regions, particularly London and the Home Counties, account for the majority of transactions in this price bracket. However, even in these traditionally strong markets, sales times have lengthened significantly:

  • Central London prime properties typically take 5-7 months to sell
  • Country homes in the Home Counties average 6-8 months on market
  • Coastal luxury properties face the longest waits at 9-12 months

Market analysts suggest that prospective buyers of high-value properties might find more room for negotiation than in previous years, whilst sellers may need to exercise patience or consider alternative marketing approaches.

As the property market continues to evolve, these trends highlight the importance of realistic pricing and understanding local market conditions, particularly for those dealing with premium properties or flats. Homeowners in these segments may wish to seek professional valuations and market advice before making decisions.

item.title: New survey shows MTD confusion
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

A recent survey has revealed widespread confusion among property investors regarding the government's Making Tax Digital (MTD) requirements, with many unaware of their upcoming obligations under the scheme.

Understanding Making Tax Digital for property

HMRC's Making Tax Digital initiative aims to modernise the tax system by requiring digital record-keeping and quarterly submissions for certain taxpayers. From April 2026, the rules will extend to landlords and property investors with annual business or property income above £50,000, with those earning between £30,000 and £50,000 following in April 2027.

Despite these impending changes, the August survey suggests many investors remain unprepared, potentially risking penalties for non-compliance. The transition requires compatible software and adjusted accounting practices that some landlords may not yet have implemented.

Key areas of confusion identified

The research highlighted several common misconceptions:

  • Nearly 40% of respondents believed the rules only applied to limited companies
  • One third thought they could continue with annual paper submissions
  • Many didn't realise the phased implementation dates applied to property income

This knowledge gap could prove problematic as the deadlines approach, particularly for landlords with multiple properties or complex portfolios who may need more time to adapt their systems.

Preparing for the MTD transition

Property investors might consider taking several steps to prepare:

  • Reviewing current record-keeping practices and identifying necessary software solutions
  • Checking HMRC's approved software list to ensure compatibility
  • Considering professional accounting advice if managing complex property finances

Those affected may wish to begin the transition well in advance of the 2026 deadline to avoid last-minute complications. HMRC offers detailed guidance on their website, including specific information for landlords and property businesses.

With significant changes to tax reporting on the horizon, staying informed about MTD requirements could help property investors avoid unnecessary penalties while potentially streamlining their financial administration in the long term.

item.title: UK short-term rental operators raised rates in Q3
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Short-term rental operators in the UK increased their rates during the third quarter of the year, according to recent data. This move appears to have helped holiday let owners maintain revenue levels despite facing challenges such as reduced occupancy rates and shifting booking patterns. The findings highlight how the holiday let market is adapting to changing consumer behaviour in the post-pandemic landscape.

Rising Rates Amid Changing Trends

The latest figures reveal that many short-term rental operators chose to raise their prices during Q3. This decision seems to have been driven by a combination of factors, including rising operational costs and a desire to offset declining occupancy rates. Whilst some homeowners might have been hesitant to increase rates, the strategy appears to have paid off for many, helping to safeguard income levels in an increasingly competitive market.

Industry analysts suggest that the rise in prices could also reflect evolving booking trends. With travellers increasingly opting for shorter stays or last-minute bookings, operators may have adjusted their pricing strategies to maximise revenue from these changing patterns. This approach could be particularly effective in popular tourist destinations, where demand remains relatively strong despite wider economic pressures.

Impact on the Holiday Let Market

The decision to raise rates comes at a time when the UK holiday let market is facing several challenges. Whilst demand for short-term rentals remains robust in certain areas, some regions have experienced a slowdown in bookings. This has led to a more competitive environment, with operators needing to find ways to attract guests whilst maintaining profitability.

For homeowners considering entering the holiday let market, these trends could offer valuable insights. Understanding how to balance pricing with occupancy levels might be key to achieving success in this sector. Additionally, staying informed about changing booking patterns could help operators tailor their offerings to meet the evolving needs of travellers.

As the market continues to adapt, it could be worth monitoring how these pricing strategies play out in the coming months. With the festive season approaching, operators may face further opportunities to adjust their rates and maximise revenue during peak periods.

Overall, the latest data suggests that UK short-term rental operators are taking proactive steps to navigate a challenging market. By raising rates and adapting to changing trends, many have managed to protect their income despite facing headwinds. For those involved in the holiday let sector, staying flexible and responsive to market conditions could remain crucial in the months ahead.

item.title: Why Reactive Repairs Are Quietly Draining Landlord Returns
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Hidden Cost of Reactive Repairs for Landlords

When landlords consider their expenses, mortgage rates, tax changes, and void periods often dominate the conversation. However, there is a less visible yet significant drain on returns: reactive repairs. These unforeseen maintenance issues, tackled on an ad-hoc basis, may seem minor in isolation. Yet, when accumulated over a year, they can substantially impact profitability.

Understanding Reactive Repairs

Reactive repairs refer to maintenance tasks addressed in response to emergencies or immediate issues. These can range from fixing a broken boiler to repairing a leaky roof. While essential for tenant satisfaction and property upkeep, such repairs often come with higher costs due to their urgent nature. Landlords may find themselves paying premium rates for emergency call-outs or last-minute materials.

The Financial Impact of Neglecting Preventative Maintenance

One of the key reasons reactive repairs become costly is the lack of preventative maintenance. Regular property inspections and proactive upkeep can help identify potential issues before they escalate into emergencies. For example, servicing a boiler annually is typically more affordable than replacing it after a sudden breakdown. Landlords might consider budgeting for routine maintenance to reduce the frequency and expense of unexpected repairs.

Whilst reactive repairs are unavoidable at times, landlords who prioritise preventative measures could see a notable improvement in their returns. By addressing small issues early and planning for regular upkeep, they may minimise the financial strain of emergency fixes and maintain healthier profit margins in the long term.

item.title: Higher mortgage costs wipe out first-time buyer savings
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

First-time buyers across the UK are facing a challenging financial landscape as rising mortgage costs increasingly outweigh former rental payments. Recent research reveals that over half (56%) of those stepping onto the property ladder in September now pay more for their mortgage than they previously did in rent - a significant jump from just 33% during the same period last year.

The shifting affordability landscape

Analysis by estate agency Hamptons shows the average first-time buyer now faces mortgage repayments of £1,227 per month - meaning they pay £1.09 in mortgage costs for every £1 they previously spent on rent. This represents a notable change from September 2022, when the ratio stood at just 90p per pound of former rent. The proportion of buyers facing higher housing costs after purchase has reached its highest level in at least ten years.

The situation has deteriorated rapidly, with fewer than half (47%) of July's first-time buyers experiencing this cost increase. The figures highlight how consecutive Bank of England base rate rises have fundamentally altered the financial equation for aspiring homeowners.

How deposit size influences affordability

The research uncovered important differences based on deposit size:

  • Buyers with higher mortgage payments typically put down 9% deposits (equivalent to 91% LTV mortgages)
  • Those whose payments fell below previous rent usually secured mortgages with 17% deposits

Age also plays a crucial role in affordability:

  • 67% of buyers in their 40s faced higher payments (average 18.2% increase)
  • 58% of 30-somethings paid more (6.9% average rise)
  • 47% of 20-somethings saw costs increase (with average payments 7.5% below former rent)

This disparity stems from older buyers generally purchasing larger properties with shorter mortgage terms - typically 27 years for those in their 40s compared to 34 years for younger purchasers.

Rental market continues to heat up

Meanwhile, the rental market shows no signs of cooling, with newly let property prices increasing for the tenth consecutive month. September saw annual rental growth reach 2.7% nationwide, pushing the average monthly rent to £1,433.

Regional variations remain pronounced, with the South East recording 4.6% growth and the South West close behind at 4.1% - both regions exceeding 4% annual rental inflation for the first time in recent memory.

For renters considering homeownership, these findings highlight the importance of carefully evaluating monthly costs, deposit options and mortgage terms. While building equity remains a powerful financial incentive, the short-term affordability picture has undoubtedly become more complex in the current market.

item.title: Landlords face ‘absurd’ tax bills on inflation
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Landlords across the UK are facing mounting calls for a reform of capital gains tax (CGT) rules, as critics argue the current system unfairly taxes inflation-driven property price increases rather than genuine gains. The National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) has urged the government to address this issue in the forthcoming Budget, warning that the existing framework discourages long-term investment in the private rented sector.

Taxing inflation: A growing concern for landlords

Under current CGT rules, landlords are taxed on the difference between a property’s purchase price and its sale price, after accounting for allowable costs and reliefs. However, the NRLA highlights that much of this apparent gain is often due to inflation rather than true increases in property value. Its analysis reveals that between 2015 and 2024, just 20% of house price growth represented real-terms gains, with inflation accounting for the remaining 80%.

Ben Beadle, chief executive of the NRLA, described the situation as “absurd,” stating: “It is absurd that investors face capital gains tax on increases in property prices that are simply the result of inflation. That’s not a real gain, and it shouldn’t be treated as one.” He argues that taxing inflation devalues investments and reduces potential returns, making it more appealing for landlords to leave their money in the bank rather than invest in rental properties.

Proposals to incentivise long-term investment

The NRLA has proposed several reforms to address these challenges. Its key recommendation is to adjust taxable property gains for inflation, effectively increasing the original purchase price and qualifying capital expenditure in line with inflation. This would mean landlords pay less CGT on price increases attributable to inflation, ensuring they are only taxed on genuine gains.

Additionally, the association suggests introducing reliefs that reflect how long landlords retain properties for rental use. Long-term investors would benefit under this system, while short-term speculators would receive no relief. Safeguards would also be implemented to prevent inflation adjustments from creating or increasing allowable capital losses.

The impact on rental supply

The call for reform comes at a time when rental supply remains under significant pressure. According to Rightmove, each available rental property attracts an average of 10 enquiries, double the pre-pandemic level. The NRLA argues that current CGT rules exacerbate this shortage by discouraging landlords from investing in the private rented sector.

Beadle emphasised the urgent need for change, stating: “All regions of this country desperately need more homes to rent, yet our tax system fails to encourage landlords to make long-term investments to provide them.” He urged the chancellor to use the upcoming Budget as an opportunity to address these issues and support the private rented sector.

As landlords await potential reforms, the debate over CGT rules highlights the delicate balance between taxation and investment in the UK’s housing market. With rental demand continuing to outstrip supply, many will be watching closely to see whether the government takes steps to encourage long-term investment in the sector.

Its analysis reveals that between 2015 and 2024, just 20% of house price growth represented real-terms gains, with inflation accounting for the remaining 80%.

Ben Beadle, chief executive of the NRLA, described the situation as “absurd,” stating: “It is absurd that investors face capital gains tax on increases in property prices that are simply the result of inflation. That’s not a real gain, and it shouldn’t be treated as one.” He argues that taxing inflation devalues investments and reduces potential returns, making it more appealing for landlords to leave their money in the bank rather than invest in rental properties.

Proposals to incentivise long-term investment

The NRLA has proposed several reforms to address these challenges. Its key recommendation is to adjust taxable property gains for inflation, effectively increasing the original purchase price and qualifying capital expenditure in line with inflation. This would mean landlords pay less CGT on price increases attributable to inflation, ensuring they are only taxed on genuine gains.

Additionally, the association suggests introducing reliefs that reflect how long landlords retain properties for rental use. Long-term investors would benefit under this system, while short-term speculators would receive no relief. Safeguards would also be implemented to prevent inflation adjustments from creating or increasing allowable capital losses.

The impact on rental supply

The call for reform comes at a time when rental supply remains under significant pressure. According to Rightmove, each available rental property attracts an average of 10 enquiries, double the pre-pandemic level. The NRLA argues that current CGT rules exacerbate this shortage by discouraging landlords from investing in the private rented sector.

Beadle emphasised the urgent need for change, stating: “All regions of this country desperately need more homes to rent, yet our tax system fails to encourage landlords to make long-term investments to provide them.” He urged the chancellor to use the upcoming Budget as an opportunity to address these issues and support the private rented sector.

As landlords await potential reforms, the debate over CGT rules highlights the delicate balance between taxation and investment in the UK’s housing market. With rental demand continuing to outstrip supply, many will be watching closely to see whether the government takes steps to encourage long-term investment in the sector.

item.title: Mortgage rate shock hits previously resilient housing markets
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Previously resilient regional housing markets are beginning to show signs of strain as rising mortgage rates take their toll on buyer affordability. According to Rightmove's latest House Price Index, four of Britain's five most affordable regions have seen sellers reduce asking prices this month, with the North East leading declines at 2%.

Affordable regions feel the squeeze

The data reveals a notable shift in market dynamics, with monthly price reductions now affecting areas that had largely resisted downward pressure earlier this year. Scotland recorded the second-largest decrease at 1.9%, followed by the North West (0.6%) and Wales (0.3%). Yorkshire and the Humber bucked the trend with a modest 0.3% increase.

This emerging pattern coincides with a sharp rise in mortgage costs, with the average two-year fixed rate reaching 5.55% this month - a significant jump from 4.25% before geopolitical tensions escalated in February. Rightmove estimates these rate rises have added approximately £250 per month to the cost of servicing a typical new mortgage.

Colleen Babcock, Rightmove's property expert, commented: "We're now seeing mortgage rate rises feed through to seller pricing in many of Britain's more affordable regions. This serves as a clear indicator that higher borrowing costs are affecting purchasing power across all market segments."

London's seasonal rebound masks underlying challenges

The capital presented a contrasting picture, recording Britain's strongest monthly price growth at 2.5%, with Inner London properties driving the increase with a 3.9% uplift. However, this follows a particularly weak summer period that saw prices drop 6% across July and August.

Analysts suggest the recent uptick partly reflects seasonal patterns, with some sellers deliberately delaying listings until autumn. Despite this monthly improvement, London's asking prices remain 1.7% below last October's levels, and market indicators suggest ongoing challenges.

Rightmove's data shows 38% of London properties have undergone price reductions since coming to market, underlining the importance of realistic initial pricing. Babcock emphasised: "Competitive pricing from day one remains critical to capitalise on buyer interest in the current climate."

Strategic pricing becomes crucial

With the market demonstrating heightened sensitivity to pricing, homeowners planning to sell might consider reviewing local market conditions carefully. The data suggests properties priced competitively from the outset stand a better chance of attracting serious buyers amidst tighter affordability constraints.

Prospective buyers, meanwhile, could find increasing opportunities for negotiation in regions showing price softening, though they'll need to balance this against higher mortgage costs. The current environment underlines the importance of thorough research and financial planning when entering the market.

As the property market navigates these changing conditions, both buyers and sellers may benefit from professional advice to understand how shifting mortgage rates and regional variations could affect their individual circumstances.

item.title: More than 3,000 asking prices slashed every day as sellers face reality
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property market is witnessing a significant shift as sellers adjust their expectations amidst rising mortgage costs and increased competition. According to recent data from Rightmove, more than 3,000 properties had their asking prices reduced each day during September, marking the fastest pace of reductions in 15 years. The average price drop was nearly 7%, equating to around £21,000 on a typically priced home. With buyer enquiries declining and sales agreed falling, the market is experiencing heightened pressure to align asking prices with current realities.

The Impact of Overpricing

Rightmove’s research underscores the challenges of launching properties at unrealistic asking prices. Homes that required a reduction spent an average of 119 days on the market before securing a buyer, compared to just 39 days for properties marketed at the right price from the outset. This means reduced properties took more than three times longer to sell. Colleen Babcock, Rightmove’s property expert, highlighted that prolonged marketing periods and subsequent price cuts can lead to buyer scepticism, even when there is no inherent issue with the property. In a market brimming with choice, first impressions and accurate pricing are more crucial than ever.

Mortgage Costs and Regional Trends

The rising cost of borrowing is adding further strain to the market. Rightmove’s latest House Price Index reveals that the average two-year fixed mortgage rate has climbed to 5.55%, up from 5.29% last month. This increase has added approximately £250 per month to the cost of a typical new mortgage, leaving many prospective buyers cautious. The impact is being felt across the UK, with four of the five lowest-priced regions recording price reductions in October. The North East saw the largest monthly fall at 2%, followed by Scotland at 1.9%. Prices also dipped in the North West (-0.6%) and Wales (-0.3%), while Yorkshire and the Humber experienced a modest 0.3% rise.

Market Dynamics and Buyer Demand

Despite these regional fluctuations, average asking prices across Britain rose by 1% in October to £371,015, though they remain 0.1% below the same period last year. However, buyer demand continues to weaken, with sales agreed running 8% lower than last year. The number of homes available for sale has also reached a 12-year seasonal high, further intensifying competition among sellers. For homeowners looking to sell, pricing their property realistically from the outset could help avoid prolonged marketing periods and attract serious buyers in a challenging market.

As the UK property market navigates these shifting dynamics, sellers may wish to carefully consider their pricing strategies and seek professional advice to ensure their homes stand out in an increasingly competitive landscape.

item.title: Mortgage rates jump again as lenders pull deals at record pace
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK mortgage market is experiencing unprecedented volatility, with lenders withdrawing deals at a record pace and rates continuing to climb. According to Moneyfacts, the average mortgage product remained on the market for just 13 days in September, down from 14 days in August. This marks a significant decline compared to previous years, with products lasting an average of 20 days in 2022 and 43 days in 2019. This instability has left borrowers and brokers racing to secure deals before they disappear.

Rising Mortgage Rates Amid Market Instability

Despite a slight increase in the number of mortgage products available, rates have been on an upward trajectory. The average two-year fixed mortgage rate rose from 5.59% in September to 5.93% in October, while the average five-year fixed rate increased from 5.63% to 5.95%. The Moneyfacts Average New Mortgage Rate also saw a jump, climbing to 5.83% in October from 5.55% the previous month.

This trend highlights the challenges facing borrowers, as lenders continue to adjust their offerings in response to fluctuating wholesale funding costs. Whilst product availability has improved since the market disruption earlier in the year, the rapid repricing and withdrawal of deals are making it difficult for homeowners to secure affordable finance.

Shorter Shelf-Life for Mortgage Products

One of the most striking aspects of the current market is the shrinking shelf-life of mortgage products. So far this year, deals have remained available for an average of just 15 days, down from 20 days in 2022. This leaves borrowers with a much narrower window to compare and secure competitive rates.

Adam French, head of consumer finance at Moneyfacts, commented on the situation, stating, “Brokers and borrowers are navigating the most challenging mortgage market in modern records. Not only have rates been jumping up and down, but the deals available today may not be here tomorrow.” He added that the prolonged instability has made 2023 particularly difficult compared to previous periods of disruption.

Implications for Borrowers and the Housing Market

The volatility in the mortgage market is creating additional uncertainty for both buyers and estate agents. Frequent product changes and rising rates are complicating affordability calculations, making it harder for buyers to plan their finances. For estate agents, the unpredictability of mortgage costs and the limited time buyers have to secure deals are adding further complexity to the home-buying process.

Homeowners may wish to act quickly if they are considering remortgaging or purchasing a new property, as deals can disappear within days. It could also be worth consulting a mortgage broker to navigate the rapidly changing landscape and secure the best possible rate.

The ongoing instability in the mortgage market underscores the importance of staying informed and acting swiftly. With deals lasting just a matter of days and rates continuing to rise, borrowers might consider seeking professional advice to ensure they secure a competitive mortgage product before it’s too late.

item.title: Property industry reacts to latest Rightmove House Price Index
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The latest Rightmove House Price Index reveals a mixed picture for the UK property market, with average asking prices rising by 1% in October to £371,015. However, this figure remains 0.1% below last year’s levels, reflecting ongoing challenges for buyers and sellers alike. With average two-year fixed mortgage rates now at 5.55% and buyer enquiries down by 9% year-on-year, the market is experiencing significant shifts. Sales agreed have also fallen by 8%, whilst the number of homes available for sale has reached its highest October level since 2014.

The Impact of Rising Mortgage Rates

The increase in mortgage rates continues to weigh heavily on buyer affordability, creating a more cautious market. Borrowers might find themselves needing to budget carefully, as higher borrowing costs reduce their purchasing power. This has led to a slowdown in market activity, with fewer sales being agreed compared to previous years. Experts suggest that buyers are prioritising affordability, ensuring they have sufficient financial headroom to cover both expected and unexpected expenses before committing to a purchase.

Industry professionals highlight that the current economic climate, including inflation and geopolitical uncertainties, is contributing to this trend. For example, the ongoing conflict in the Middle East has added further pressure, with potential implications for global markets and UK borrowing costs. Homeowners may wish to keep a close eye on these developments, as any de-escalation could lead to a swift reversal in mortgage rates.

The Importance of Competitive Pricing for Sellers

In this challenging environment, sellers are being advised to set realistic asking prices to attract buyers. Estate agents report that properties priced competitively are more likely to stand out in a crowded market. With the number of homes for sale at an eight-year high for October, sellers who recognise the need to adapt to current conditions are finding greater success.

Jeremy Leaf, a north London estate agent and former RICS residential chairman, notes that sensitivity to pricing is crucial. He explains that whilst sales are gaining some momentum, buyers remain cautious, and only competitively priced properties are securing interest. This underscores the importance of accurate valuation and a willingness to negotiate in today’s market.

Looking Ahead: Budget Uncertainties and Market Outlook

The upcoming Budget announcement is another factor adding to the uncertainty in the property market. Potential tax changes, including those affecting banks, could further influence mortgage rates and buyer confidence. Tomer Aboody, founding director of MT Finance, suggests that this combination of higher mortgage rates, tax concerns, and rising inflation is keeping a lid on property values.

Tom Bill, head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, adds that the outlook for next year remains uncertain. He explains that the housing market’s performance will largely depend on geopolitical developments and their impact on borrowing costs. Borrowers and sellers alike may wish to stay informed and seek professional advice to navigate these complexities effectively.

In summary, the UK property market is facing a period of adjustment, with rising mortgage rates and economic uncertainties influencing buyer and seller behaviour. Competitive pricing and careful financial planning could be key to success in the months ahead.

item.title: Sellers flood the market as agreed property sales slump
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK property market has experienced a significant shift in recent months, with a growing disparity between the number of homes coming onto the market and those being sold. According to data from property analytics firm Sprift, September saw 213,048 new listings across Great Britain, marking a 14.8% increase from August. However, agreed sales fell sharply by 16.1% to 89,192, leaving a gap of 123,856 between new instructions and completed transactions. This imbalance has raised concerns about buyer demand and its potential impact on property prices.

Regional Variations in Market Performance

The data reveals striking regional differences in market activity. Scotland emerged as the strongest performer, with a sales conversion rate of 69.5%, the highest across the UK. In contrast, London struggled, achieving just a 27% conversion rate. This regional gap of 42.5 percentage points highlights the varying dynamics at play. Northern England, the Midlands, and Wales also outperformed the national average, while southern regions, including London and the South East, lagged behind.

London experienced a 28.7% surge in new listings, but agreed sales declined by 14.8%, creating a gap of 20,868 properties. The South East recorded the largest regional disparity, with 23,253 more homes coming onto the market than those sold. Together, these two regions accounted for approximately a third of the UK’s available housing stock. Both areas also saw high levels of price reductions, with 43.7% of properties in the South East and 40.9% in London undergoing price adjustments.

Impact of Rising Mortgage Rates

The slowdown in sales coincides with rising mortgage costs, which may be deterring potential buyers. By 1 October, the average two-year fixed mortgage rate had climbed to 5.93%, while the effective rate on newly drawn mortgages increased from 4.45% to 4.60%. Mortgage approvals for house purchases also fell to 54,900 in August, their lowest level since December 2023. These rising borrowing costs could be contributing to the reduced buyer activity and slower sales conversion rates.

Property Type Trends

The market slowdown has been particularly pronounced for larger properties. Listings of detached homes with five or more bedrooms surged by 36.3% in September, but their sales conversion rate plummeted from 51.7% to 31.9% in just one month. On the other hand, smaller properties like two-bedroom bungalows performed better, achieving a conversion rate of 61.4%, the highest among all property categories.

Selling times also varied significantly across regions and property types. Semi-detached homes in Scotland spent an average of 99.3 days on the market, the shortest period among the categories examined. Flats and smaller properties generally fared better, suggesting that affordability and practicality remain key considerations for buyers in the current climate.

As the UK property market navigates these challenges, homeowners may wish to carefully assess local market conditions and seek professional advice to understand their options. With regional variations and rising mortgage costs shaping buyer behaviour, staying informed could be crucial for those looking to buy or sell in the coming months.
